questions.question: Climbers near the top of Mount Everest, almost 9 kilometres above sea level, cross grey limestone that holds fossils of crinoids, the animals called sea lilies. Crinoids live only in the sea. How did their fossils come to be so high?
questions.answer: Old sea floor was later pushed up into mountains
choices: Old sea floor was later pushed up into mountains
The sea once rose higher than the mountain's top
A great flood once swept them up the mountain
Their shapes grew inside the mountain's rock
questions.context: The limestone formed about 450 million years ago on the floor of a warm, shallow sea, and long afterward the rock was thrust up kilometres high as the mountains were built. The sea has never stood more than a few hundred metres above today's level, far short of the summit. Leonardo da Vinci, some 500 years ago, already doubted that a flood had carried such shells there, and argued that they were laid down in ancient seas.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards (TEKS 7.10A) teach sea fossils high in mountains as evidence that Earth's surface has changed, a step past the fifth-grade idea that a sea once covered the land.

questions.question: Fossil leaves of Glossopteris, a seed fern, lie in rocks of the same age in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica. Wide oceans lie between those lands. What best explains how one kind of plant came to grow on all five?
questions.answer: The lands were once joined together
choices: The lands were once joined together
The plant arose on each land by itself
Birds carried its seeds from land to land
Sea currents floated its seeds to each land
questions.context: Glossopteris seeds were far too big to blow across thousands of kilometres of open sea, floating that far was unlikely, and the first birds appeared some 100 million years after the plant had died out. Nor does one kind of plant arise all by itself, by chance, on five separate lands. Glossopteris could spread across all five only while they were joined together.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the same fossil species on continents now oceans apart (Glossopteris is the textbook case) as evidence that the continents were once joined (TEKS 7.10A, NGSS MS-ESS2-3).

questions.question: Geologists find fossils of one kind of living thing on two coasts that face each other across an ocean. Fossils of which kind of living thing would give the strongest evidence that the two lands were once joined?
questions.answer: A plant-eating reptile as big as a pig
choices: A plant-eating reptile as big as a pig
A shark as long as a small rowing boat
A seabird as big as a farmyard goose
A fern as tall as a grown man
questions.context: Lystrosaurus, a plant-eating reptile of dry land about as big as a pig, has been dug up in South Africa, India and Antarctica, and Mesosaurus, a small reptile of shallow coastal water, only in southern Africa and eastern South America. Neither could have crossed an open ocean, so finding them on both sides means the lands were once connected. Sharks swim across oceans and seabirds fly over them, and ferns make no seeds but tiny spores that the wind carries hundreds of kilometres, even across oceans, so their fossils on two coasts show little.
questions.grade_note: NGSS MS-ESS2-3 asks seventh graders to interpret the spread of fossils across continents as evidence, which means judging which fossils count: the reptiles and land animals of the southern continents.

questions.question: Geologists working in the mountains of Antarctica, a land buried under thick ice, find seam after seam of coal in the bare rock. What does the coal show about Antarctica long ago?
questions.answer: Swamp forests grew in a mild, wet climate
choices: Swamp forests grew in a mild, wet climate
Volcanoes poured black lava across it
Dry sand dunes covered it, as in a desert
A warm, shallow sea covered all of it
questions.context: Coal forms from the remains of plants that piled up in waterlogged swamps and were buried, so the coal means forests once grew where ice lies now. Many were Glossopteris trees, which grew there about 250 to 300 million years ago in a climate far milder than today's. Coal is a black rock made of plants, not hardened lava, and it cannot form among desert dunes or on a sea floor.
questions.grade_note: Coal in Antarctica is a standard seventh-grade piece of evidence that Earth has changed (TEKS 7.10A), applying the earlier fact that coal comes from ancient swamp plants.

questions.question: The Appalachian Mountains of North America and the old mountains of Scotland and Norway are built of the same kinds of rock, formed at the same time and folded in the same way. The Atlantic Ocean lies between them. What best explains the match?
questions.answer: They formed as one range that later split
choices: They formed as one range that later split
A shrinking Earth wrinkled both at once
One worldwide sea laid the same rock in both
One great earthquake pushed both up at once
questions.context: Before the Atlantic opened, these mountains were one long range, built over many millions of years, and when the land split apart, its pieces ended up on both sides of the new ocean. Abraham Werner, a German mineralogist of the 1700s, taught that one worldwide sea had laid down the same rocks everywhere, and geologists of the 1800s thought a cooling, shrinking Earth wrinkled up its mountains like the skin of a drying apple, but the evidence led geologists to give up both ideas.
questions.grade_note: Matching rocks and mountain belts across oceans are named in seventh-grade standards (NGSS MS-ESS2-3) as evidence that continents have moved.

questions.question: A cliff shows three flat, unbroken layers of rock. On top lies sandstone made from the sand of desert dunes, in the middle a seam of coal, and at the bottom limestone packed with seashells. What was this spot, from first to last?
questions.answer: Sea, then swamp forest, then desert
choices: Sea, then swamp forest, then desert
Desert, then swamp forest, then sea
Swamp forest, then sea, then desert
Sea, then desert, then swamp forest
questions.context: In layers that lie as they formed, each one settled on top of the ones already there, so the bottom layer is the oldest and the top one the youngest. This spot was first a sea floor, then a swamp forest whose plants became coal, and last a desert of drifting dunes. Reading the cliff from the top down tells the story backwards.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches superposition, the oldest layer at the bottom of undisturbed rock, and uses it with fossils to read how a place changed (TEKS 7.10A).

questions.question: Along a sea cliff, layers of sandstone and shale stand almost on end, as steep as a wall. The sand and mud in them settled out of water long ago. How did the layers come to stand so steeply?
questions.answer: They settled flat and were tilted later
choices: They settled flat and were tilted later
Ice in their cracks pushed them upright
They settled on a steep slope and hardened
Waves wore the flat layers into a slant
questions.context: Sand and mud settle in flat or nearly flat layers, and even the steepest slopes they build, on the fronts of deltas and dunes, lean only about 20 to 35 degrees. Layers that stand on end were tilted by forces in Earth's crust long after they formed. Ice freezing in cracks can split rock and break off blocks near the surface, but it cannot stand whole layers on end.
questions.grade_note: Middle-school Earth science teaches that sedimentary layers form flat, so tilted layers must have moved after they formed.

questions.question: A road cut through a hill shows six flat layers of rock. A crack, called a fault, runs up through the four lowest layers, which have all slipped a metre lower on one side of it. The two layers above them lie flat and unbroken across the crack. When did the fault form?
questions.answer: After the bottom four, before the top two
choices: After the bottom four, before the top two
After the top two, before the bottom four
After all six layers had formed
While the bottom four were forming
questions.context: A layer has to exist before it can be broken, so the fault is younger than the four layers it cuts, and since they all slipped the same metre, all four were already there when it moved. The two layers above lie flat and unbroken across it, so they settled after the fault had formed, and layers settle from the bottom up. So the fault formed after the bottom four and before the top two.
questions.grade_note: Middle-school Earth science teaches that a fault is younger than the layers it cuts and older than layers that lie unbroken across it, read together with superposition.

questions.question: A geologist reading the layers of a cliff usually takes the bottom layer to be the oldest. Before she trusts that rule, what must she first make sure of?
questions.answer: That the layers have not been flipped over
choices: That the layers have not been flipped over
That no layer has been worn away by erosion
That every layer formed under the sea
That each layer took the same time to form
questions.context: Squeezing can fold a stack of layers so far that it turns upside down, putting the oldest layer on top, and a fault can push older rock over younger, so a geologist looks for folds and faults first. A layer worn away leaves a gap but does not change the order of the layers that are left, and layers laid down by wind on land stack up the same way as those laid in the sea. The rule gives only the order, not how long each layer took to form.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards teach superposition for undisturbed layers, and the condition, that folding can overturn layers, is part of using it.

eeebb0bba2.why: Judge (medium): three wrong choices were one kind (wind, birds or currents carried the seeds), so the odd one out won, and 'Today wide oceans part those lands' hinted it was not always so. Per the judge's fix the stem now says 'Wide oceans lie between those lands', and the wind choice is replaced by the alternative a student might reach for, 'The plant arose on each land by itself' (independent origin, which the Geological Society of London treats as unlikely; F26, sourced now). The context says why each is wrong.

23736dfd81.why: Judge (high): every choice carried its own answer ('roamed the open ocean', 'flew far over the sea', 'tiny spores rode the wind', 'lived only on dry land'), so the question tested nothing. Per the judge's fix the choices are now four plain, parallel creatures with no crossing cue (a size for each), so the student must know which can cross an ocean on its own; the fern is the lure that needs knowledge, since ferns spread by wind-blown spores across oceans. The judge's 'tree fern' is now 'a fern', so it is not mistaken for a tree like Glossopteris. Facts sourced now (F27). Stem unchanged, so the hash is the same.

65d31b180e.why: Judge (medium): 'Thick ice covered it, much as it does now' was the no-change choice in a question about long ago, struck at once. Per the judge's fix it is replaced by a real mix-up about black rock, 'Volcanoes poured black lava across it' (coal is a sedimentary rock made of plants, F28, sourced now); the context says so. Stem unchanged, so the hash is the same.

a44c1dd82e.why: Judge (medium): 'They rose apart and came out alike by chance' could not stand against the stem's matching rocks, age and folding, and 'Glaciers dragged rock from one to the other' across an ocean was not live. They are replaced by the respectable wrong idea of the contracting Earth, 'A shrinking Earth wrinkled both at once', and the sudden-uplift mix-up, 'One great earthquake pushed both up at once' (mountain belts are built over many millions of years); the judge's 'same kind of magma rose under both' was not used, since mountain building does bring up magma and the choice could be argued as partly true. Facts sourced now (F29). The context names both old ideas.

c9f9828312.why: Judge (medium): the stem listed the layers bottom first, so the key just read the stem's order back. Per the judge's fix the stem now lists them top first, so a student who reads the cliff the way it is listed lands on the lure 'Desert, then swamp forest, then sea' and must apply superposition to reach the key. Choices and context unchanged.

5d9485919c.why: Judge (low, taken as cheap and safe): 'They settled on end, just as they stand now' was not a picture any student holds. Replaced with frost wedging misapplied, 'Ice in their cracks pushed them upright' (ice splits rock near the surface but does not stand whole layers on end, F30, sourced now); the context says so. Stem unchanged, so the hash is the same.

60b441b210.why: Judge (medium): the stem said the crack 'runs through all six' and the key repeated 'all six', and the two 'while ... forming' choices were dead, so plain logic settled a two-way choice. Per the judge's fix the fault now cuts only the four lowest layers and the top two lie unbroken across it, so the student must combine superposition (layers settle from the bottom up) with cross-cutting (a fault is younger than what it cuts, older than what lies unbroken over it). The choices are the key, its mirror for a student who reads the cliff top-down ('After the top two, before the bottom four'), cross-cutting over-applied ('After all six layers had formed') and a fault growing as the layers formed ('While the bottom four were forming', ruled out because all four slipped the same metre, F31, sourced now). The stem's 'four lowest' and 'two layers above them' keep it from sharing a phrase with the key.

a51b4b684c.why: Judge (medium): the three wrong conditions (thickest bottom layer, most fossils, one colour) had nothing to do with order and no student thinks a geologist checks them, so the key won by elimination. They are replaced by conditions a student might really think the rule needs, which it does not: 'That no layer has been worn away by erosion' and 'That every layer formed under the sea' (the judge's), and 'That each layer took the same time to form' (the judge's 'all of one kind of rock' was not used: superposition does not hold for igneous rock pushed in later between layers, F32's source, so it was partly defensible). Fact-check's optional rewording taken: the context no longer says the rule holds 'only where the layers still lie as they formed'; it names folds and faults (F20, F32, sourced now). Stem and key unchanged, so the hash is the same.
